text.tspan: A calendar gives plans a place in time.
A useful routine should fit real life. I learned that choosing one realistic priority and returning after interruptions work better than
making an ambitious plan I cannot keep.
First, a small priority is easier to act on. I used to plan several new activities every day, but I usually fell behind. Then I chose ten
minutes of reading after dinner and put a book beside my chair. The clear, simple task was easier to remember.
Second, a flexible routine survives ordinary interruptions. Sometimes a visitor arrived or another task took longer than expected.
Instead of giving up, I returned to reading the next evening. Missing one day did not mean abandoning the whole plan.
Realistic goals and flexible expectations helped reading become part of my day. A routine does not need to be impressive to be
useful. It succeeds when it is simple enough to start and forgiving enough to continue.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each
body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a
Identify two obstacles that could arise when people make a realistic plan. Explain a workable response to each, rather than merely
listing the problems. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline:
introduce the situation; discuss reviewing a specific experience teaches more than a vague judgement with an example; discuss a
small next step is easier to act on than a broad promise with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
